sections.h: The three guards and the return (1 Esdras 3-5)
sections.b: The heart of 1 Esdras is a story no Hebrew book has. At a feast of Darius, three young bodyguards write what is strongest: wine, the king, women, and truth over all (1 Esdras 3:10-12). After the speeches the people cry, "Great is truth, and it is strongest!" (1 Esdras 4:41). The winner, named in an aside as Zerubbabel (1 Esdras 4:13), asks Darius to keep his vow to rebuild Jerusalem, and receives letters, money and safe conduct (1 Esdras 4:42-57). Then the book copies the list of returnees from Ezra 2 with many changes of names and numbers, and tells the altar, the foundation and the neighbors' offer as in Ezra 3:1-4:5 (1 Esdras 5:7-70). Placing the return under Darius ties a knot in the chronology: the same chapter ends with the work stopped until Darius's reign (1 Esdras 5:70).

common: Torrey (1910) held that the contest of the three guards was a separate tale, set into the history by a later hand; Böhler reports that the truth speech is widely seen as a later addition.
uncommon: Dieter Böhler argues that the speeches on women and truth only together make one argument, and that 1 Esdras, written in the 100s BC, uses truth against the "liars" of the Hasmonean leadership.

sections.h: "Great is truth": the contest of 1 Esdras
sections.b: In 1 Esdras the third guard at Darius's court argues that truth is stronger than wine, the king and women. It lives and rules forever, shows no favorites and takes no bribes, and has strength, royal power and majesty; the speech ends, "Blessed be the God of truth!" (1 Esdras 4:35-40). The people cry, "Great is truth, and it is strongest!" (1 Esdras 4:41), in Latin magna veritas et praevalet, which as magna est veritas et praevalet became what Swete called "the immortal proverb." The same Greek word names the Thummim, "the Showing and the Truth" on the high priest's breastpiece (1 Esdras 5:40; Exodus 28:30).

claude.title: Truth told like Wisdom
claude.body: Claude's suggestion: 1 Esdras 4 praises truth the way Proverbs 8 praises Wisdom, as almost a person beside God, more precious than gold and ruling over kings. John's Gospel joins the two lines when it calls the Word "full of grace and truth" and Jesus "the truth."

sections.b: 1 Esdras makes Zerubbabel one of Darius's three young bodyguards, who wins a contest of wisdom and uses the prize to ask for Jerusalem's rebuilding (1 Esdras 4:13-57). It then lists a "Joakim son of Zerubbabel" among the priests and dates the return to Darius's second year (1 Esdras 5:5-6), which reads like a damaged text; 1 Chronicles 3:19 gives Zerubbabel's sons as Meshullam and Hananiah, and Nehemiah 12:10 makes Joiakim the son of Jeshua. Josephus follows the contest story and calls Zerubbabel an old friend of the king.

The first guard in Darius's contest argues that wine is strongest: it leads the mind astray, makes king and orphan alike, wipes out grief and debt, and ends in swords and forgetting (1 Esdras 3:17-23). The contest ranks it lowest, and the truth speech calls it "unjust" (1 Esdras 4:37). Yet the story ends with the exiles' week-long drinking feast of thanks (1 Esdras 4:63): wine in its place is joy.

Darius's second guard argues that the king is strongest because men kill, build, plant and pay taxes at his word, while he only eats and sleeps (1 Esdras 4:1-12). The third guard answers that the king is ruled by a concubine, and truth above all; the young man then calls God "the King of heaven" (1 Esdras 4:46, 58).

sections.h: A man and his wife in the speech for women (1 Esdras 4)
sections.b: Zerubbabel's speech for women uses the sense of Genesis 2:24: a man leaves his father and his country "and he sticks close to his own wife" (1 Esdras 4:20), and "a man loves his own wife far more than father and mother" (1 Esdras 4:25). The speech turns the bond of marriage into proof of women's power over men, and warns that many have lost their minds and sinned because of women (1 Esdras 4:26-27).

1 Esdras 3-4 pictures Darius I's court: a feast for 127 satrapies from India to Ethiopia, bodyguards, nobles of Persia and Media, the court rank of Kinsman, and royal letters to treasurers and satraps granting safe conduct, timber, tax freedom and money for the Jerusalem temple (1 Esdras 3:1-14; 4:42-57). The details mix Persian and later Greek usage (Coele-Syria and Phoenicia, 1 Esdras 4:48).

sections.h: The altar and the foundation in 1 Esdras
sections.b: 1 Esdras retells Ezra 3 with differences: the people gather by the east gate (1 Esdras 5:46), foreigners join at the altar (1 Esdras 5:49), the foundation is dated to the new moon of the second month (1 Esdras 5:55), and the old men's weeping drowns the trumpets (1 Esdras 5:62).

sections.h: The third copy of the return list
sections.b: 1 Esdras 5:7-45 is the third copy of the list of Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7, in Greek forms of the names, with many numbers changed, a few clans added and others missing, and the same total of 42,360. In places Hebrew place names became persons in Greek (1 Esdras 5:36), and a Persian title became a name (1 Esdras 5:40).

sections.h: The neighbors' offer in 1 Esdras and Josephus
sections.b: 1 Esdras tells the neighbors' offer as Ezra does, but names the Assyrian king Asbakaphath and has the leaders say "we alone will build" (1 Esdras 5:63-70). Josephus, following this account, calls the neighbors Cuthites, brought by "Shalmanezer" (Antiquities 11.84-88).

sections.h: "The Edomites set it on fire" (1 Esdras 4:45)
sections.b: In 1 Esdras Zerubbabel reminds Darius of the temple that "the Edomites set on fire" when the Chaldeans laid Judea waste (1 Esdras 4:45, Codex Alexandrinus; Vaticanus has "the Jews"). 2 Kings 25:9 credits the burning to Nebuchadnezzar's commander, and Obadiah and Psalm 137:7 remember Edom's part in the fall.
